#9752. NVIDIA's CEO Shake-Up Exposes a Costly Prediction Market Deadline

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

This week’s PF Weekly found it hard to ignore what is happening at NVIDIA. Jensen Huang resigned, and finance chief Colette Kress took over while the board looks for a permanent CEO. The trade that caught our eye was Kalshi’s “Before Nov 12, 2026” contract.

A Yes share paid $1 only if Huang had left as CEO and his departure had been announced by the end of Wednesday, 11 November, Eastern time. Yes traded as high as 90¢ that night. It paid zero.

At 9:11 p.m. ET on Wednesday, buyers on Kalshi paid about $12,870 for 15,500 Yes shares on that midnight deadline in seven seconds, at prices from 78¢ to 90¢. The price was back near 50¢ within half a minute. By midnight it was down to 1¢. Kalshi’s separate contract on an exit by year-end was still at 83¢.

The final hour was the busiest for the midnight contract. Some 2.38 million contracts changed hands. Open interest, the number of contracts still outstanding, rose from 2.95 million to 4.14 million even as the Yes price fell.

NVIDIA’s SEC filing says the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday, effective immediately. The company announced it at 8:48 a.m. ET on Thursday, after Kalshi’s cutoff. Polymarket’s “by November 12” contract included Thursday, so its Yes shares paid $1.

Kalshi’s two earliest deadlines accounted for 11.24 million of the 19.84 million contracts traded on Huang’s exit, or 57%. On Polymarket, the first two deadlines drew $13.18 million of the $22.73 million in reported volume, or 58%.

On Polymarket, NVIDIA’s price to finish 2026 as the world’s most valuable company fell from 64¢ on 3 November to 22¢ by Wednesday’s stock-market close, then to 11¢ by Thursday’s close. Apple went from about 35¢ to 86¢ over the same stretch. Roughly four-fifths of NVIDIA’s drop in that contract had happened before the resignation announcement. Investors were already questioning how the AI buildout would be financed.

For December 2027, I’d start with the gap in market value. Apple ended Thursday at about $5.16 trillion and NVIDIA at $4.01 trillion. If Apple stays flat, NVIDIA needs to gain about 29% to draw level. If Apple gains 10%, NVIDIA needs about 42%. If Apple loses 10%, NVIDIA needs about 16%. That cushion makes Apple my starting favourite for 2027. Microsoft ended Thursday only about 3% behind NVIDIA, so the race could get tighter from behind as well.

NVIDIA executive Ian Buck led the permanent CEO markets on Kalshi and Polymarket at about 30% in the Friday snapshots we checked. Kalshi put the chance of a permanent appointment being announced at about one in five before 1 January and close to two in three before 1 February. Kress is already running the company, and 17 November will be NVIDIA’s first earnings call with her as interim CEO.

Back in August, NVIDIA guided to $108 billion in quarterly revenue and gave a preliminary outlook for roughly 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which covers most of calendar 2027. I’ll be listening for whether Kress still expects that pace of growth and whether shipments of its new Vera Rubin systems are on schedule.

The succession market gives us a read on who might lead NVIDIA next. Tuesday’s call gives us the first chance to see whether the business is still on course to close the gap with Apple.

#9750. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9749. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9747. What Does "use client" Actually Mean in Next.js?

Frontend developer. I chase weird JavaScript, React and Next.js bugs down to the real cause, then write the story. More at bitlyst.blog

Frontend developer. I chase weird JavaScript, React and Next.js bugs down to the real cause, then write the story. More at bitlyst.blog

Frontend developer. I chase weird JavaScript, React and Next.js bugs down to the real cause, then write the story. More at bitlyst.blog

Load the page, and the message appears in the terminal where Next.js runs, not just in the browser console.

So "use client" doesn't mean "runs only in the browser". It means something else, and once you see what, it's clear where to put it.

Both kinds of component render on the server first, so the browser gets real HTML. The difference is what gets sent along with it:

The result is enough to look at. The code is what lets a component react: to clicks, typing, state and effects.

In the Next.js App Router, every component is a Server Component by default.

A Server Component runs only on the server, at build time or per request. It can be async, read a database or a file, and use secret keys. Its result is sent to the browser. Its code is never sent. A heavy library used only inside a Server Component adds zero bytes to your bundle.

A Client Component also renders on the server for the first HTML. Then its JavaScript is downloaded and React hydrates it: attaches event handlers and starts its state, so the HTML becomes interactive.

"use client" marks a boundary. The file with the directive, and everything it imports, goes into the browser bundle. You only write it at the entry point. The components it imports are client code automatically.

Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component have to travel over the network, so they must be serializable: strings, numbers, plain objects, arrays, dates, and a few more. A regular function can't be sent:

A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can receive one as children:

 is rendered on the server, and Modal only gets its result. That's how a client-side wrapper (a modal, a tab panel, a theme provider) can hold server-rendered content.

Push "use client" down to the leaves. The usual mistake is putting it at the top of a whole page because one button needs onClick:

Now only the button's code ships. The page, the data fetching and everything PostBody imports stay on the server.

This blog works that way. Each post's MDX is compiled, and every code block is syntax-highlighted, inside a Server Component. I checked the production build: the browser chunks contain highlight.js's CSS theme, but none of its JavaScript. Readers get colored code without downloading a highlighter.

Honest stakes: a Client Component in the wrong place still works. It costs bundle size and hydration time, which you feel on slow phones and big pages. Moving one "use client" from a page to a button is often the cheapest performance fix in an App Router project.

Advanced and optional. Everything above is enough to explain this in an interview. This part is for the curious: full numbers, edge cases and what's still unproven.

On the server, Next.js renders Server Components into the RSC Payload, a compact description of the rendered tree. It holds:

On the first load, Next.js uses the payload plus the Client Components to produce HTML, so the page shows before any JavaScript runs. Then the browser loads the client JavaScript, React reads the payload, and hydrates the Client Components.

On later navigations, the browser only fetches the RSC Payload for the new route (often prefetched) and React updates the page without a full reload.

There's no directive for "this is a Server Component", because that's the default. "use server" marks Server Functions: functions the client can call, which run on the server. They're the one kind of function you can pass as a prop to a Client Component, because React sends a reference to them, not their code.

createContext and providers are client-only. Make a small Client Component that renders the provider around children, and use it in a Server Component layout. Render it as deep in the tree as you can, so more of the page stays static.

A package component that uses hooks but doesn't ship "use client" breaks when rendered from a Server Component. Fix it with a one-line wrapper:

Only variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are included in client code. Others are replaced with an empty string in the browser bundle, so a secret used in a Client Component reads as empty, which is a hint it's in the wrong place.

The highlight.js check above confirms the highlighter's JavaScript is not in the browser chunks of this blog's production build. It isn't a measurement of how many kilobytes it would cost if it were shipped.

Frontend developer. I chase weird JavaScript, React and Next.js bugs down to the real cause, then write the story. More at bitlyst.blog

#9746. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9745. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog

#9744. Why Microsoft's Outlook Outage Lasted More Than 27 Hours

40+ products to market, Bell Labs to an FDA De Novo surgical robot. Fractional CPO.

40+ products to market, Bell Labs to an FDA De Novo surgical robot. Fractional CPO.

40+ products to market, Bell Labs to an FDA De Novo surgical robot. Fractional CPO.

If you use Microsoft email for business or personal use, you may have noticed a small glitch on Thursday as the email service went down. After a while, it became clear that this wasn’t a little glitch.

At 6:04 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, November 12, Microsoft’s status account posted that it was returning a portion of affected servers to the service, that they remained stable so far, and that “users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect.” Outlook had been failing for work and school accounts since a little after noon. If you were refreshing that account from an IT desk, it read like the end of a long afternoon.

At 7:06 p.m. Microsoft posted again: “The servers we returned to service can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic.”

Servers Microsoft had just brought back were falling over again, and what knocked them down was everyone trying to reach them at once. By one outside measure, traffic to Exchange Online, the service behind Outlook at work, ran about 85% below normal for roughly 18 hours. Most business customers had email again by Friday morning, and Microsoft was still restoring the rest that afternoon.

Microsoft runs one of the largest clouds on the planet. So why couldn't it just turn Outlook back on? Because the way back up turned out to be harder than the way down.

Kentik, a company that measures internet traffic, puts the start at about 12:35 p.m. Eastern. Microsoft’s first public post came at 12:54 p.m. and described trouble reaching Exchange Online mailboxes “through multiple connection methods in the Americas.” It wasn't confined to the Americas for long. CNN reported that Downdetector, the site where people go to complain about outages, logged reports from 74 countries and territories in about an hour.

In Britain, where at least one police force said it couldn’t receive online form submissions, CNN reported that police urged the public to call 101, the non-emergency number, if a problem was “time-critical but not an emergency.” The National Health Service told patients to attend their appointments as normal, Air India temporarily rerouted its email (its flights weren’t affected), and at least one company pushed back its quarterly earnings, according to CNBC. Email users, including myself, were confused because other parts of Microsoft communication services were working just fine. Teams kept working for chat and meetings, though anything inside it that depended on Exchange, like the calendar, could fail. That’s how I found out, over Teams chat with a colleague, that the email server was down for everyone.

On r/sysadmin, one administrator kept a running log of Microsoft's status updates, each followed by a deadpan “Translation” that added some much-appreciated entertainment to the situation, and one reply asked whether anyone had tried turning the entirety of Microsoft off and then on again. Canva posted a fake blue error screen announcing that some software company had run into a problem. On Hacker News, people noticed that Microsoft's own status page was throwing errors, and someone suggested the status page needed a status page.

Microsoft hasn’t published a count of the people affected, so the available figures only bracket it. At the low end, Downdetector peaked at more than 130,000 reports about Outlook. It counts only people who went to a website to complain, and as Al Jazeera pointed out, “the true number is likely far higher.” At the other end sits Microsoft's customer base: more than 450 million paid commercial seats, the figure it reported in January, according to Office 365 for IT Pros. Only part of that base was hit, because this failure was centered on Exchange.

In between, Anderson Economic Group, a Michigan research firm, gave CNN an estimate: perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million on Friday had their operations disrupted “in a way that caused an economic loss,” and the lost productivity could approach $7 billion. Its president, Patrick Anderson, was clear about the limits: “This is a starting point, with all the limitations on what we know. We don't know complete scale.”

Microsoft's first explanation that afternoon was “elevated load,” which sounds like a crowd showing up. At 2:31 p.m. it corrected that: “the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure.”

The servers that dropped out were failing what Microsoft calls automated health checks. A health check is a small, routine test a load balancer runs against each server: are you answering, and answering correctly? A server that fails gets pulled out of rotation, and its traffic goes to the ones that passed. Picture a grocery store the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, with a manager watching every checkout lane. A lane stops moving, the manager closes it, and its line gets sent elsewhere. Most of the time this is the system protecting you from a broken machine.

By 3:19 p.m. Microsoft had a new theory. It said the failed health checks “may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.” If that's right, the manager was closing lanes that were moving fine. Around 4 p.m. it said it had validated “an alternative service health check method,” and some servers came back.

Every lane that closes sends its shoppers to the lanes still open. On Thursday, the servers still in service had a weak point of their own: each connection from a phone or laptop begins with a secure handshake, the quick exchange that sets up encryption. CIO reported that the server process handling those handshakes was being overwhelmed, “causing the servers to stop processing requests.” At 5:09 p.m. Microsoft posted that “our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” and that “a core process on affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, causing capacity loss.”

An overwhelmed server answers health checks slowly or not at all, so it gets pulled too, and its share of the crowd moves to the next lane. Google’s site reliability engineers describe this spiral in the chapter of their book on cascading failures, including the case where “health-checking itself makes the service unhealthy.”

The crowd also wasn’t standing still. Outlook on your phone doesn’t give up when it can’t connect. It tries again, and so does every laptop, tablet, sync client and mail server that has a message to deliver. I may be an outlier personally, but I have two computers, a phone, and two tablets, all configured to my Outlook account, so all of them are checking, and that’s just for one person’s account. Kentik’s data, as PPC Land reported it, showed devices opening up to 70% more connections to Exchange than expected, while responses coming back from Microsoft fell to about 27% of normal. Cloudflare saw requests to Exchange Online roughly triple, “likely clients and apps retrying,” in its words.

Marc Brooker, an engineer at Amazon Web Services, wrote the standard explainer on this in Amazon's Builders’ Library. His one-line summary is “Retries are ‘selfish.’” Each client that retries is doing the sensible thing for itself, and the sum of all those sensible decisions is extra load on a system that’s already struggling. He also warns that retries “can even delay recovery by keeping the load high long after the original issue is resolved.”

In Kentik’s chart, connection attempts peaked shortly after 1 p.m. Eastern, eased off, and then spiked again at about 7:30 p.m., right after Microsoft started returning servers. Doug Madory, Kentik’s director of internet analysis, wrote that this was “the retry pressure Microsoft described as overwhelming servers once they came back online.”

That second spike came less than half an hour after Microsoft's 7:06 p.m. warning that returned servers could fail again under traffic. Bringing a server back at this scale means reopening it into a crowd that has been building for hours: every phone that’s been retrying, every queued message, every user bounced off a sick machine. They all find the first healthy server at once. Engineers call this a thundering herd. In the store, it’s the manager reopening one lane on Thanksgiving Wednesday and watching every cart in the building turn toward it.

Google’s SRE book describes servers in this spot being “bombarded with an extremely high rate of requests” the moment they come back online, until they “fail almost immediately.” Microsoft's own 7:06 p.m. post said it was “temporarily limiting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure.” At 10:13 p.m. it posted that its changes weren't “taking as expected,” and by Friday morning in Europe, Al Jazeera reported that servers Microsoft had restored were failing again.

In 2021, Nathan Bronson and three co-authors gave this pattern a name, metastable failure: a trigger “causes the system to enter a bad state that persists even when the trigger is removed,” and a feedback loop holds it there. Their first example of that loop is the one Kentik measured: “One of the most common failure-sustaining mechanisms is request retries.” Getting out, they wrote, “requires a strong corrective push, such as rebooting the system or dramatically reducing the load.”

A follow-up study at OSDI in 2022 went looking for these failures in the wild and found 22 of them across 11 organizations, four at Azure. Retries were the most common way they kept going, in more than half the incidents. The authors also noted that engineers’ first instinct, fixing the trigger, often doesn't help, because “once in the metastable failure state, the system cannot recover all by itself.”

Microsoft hasn't called this a metastable failure, and its report hasn't confirmed a retry loop. What the public record shows matches the pattern in those papers: a failure that outlived its first fix, servers that fell over again under returning traffic, and outside measurements of a retry surge that spiked when they came back.

When Facebook went dark in October 2021, its engineers wrote afterward that once the network was back, “flipping our services back on all at once could potentially cause a new round of crashes due to a surge in traffic,” so they brought load back deliberately. Two months later, Amazon’s own write-up of a major outage in its Virginia region described a capacity-scaling change that set off “a large surge of connection activity,” which produced “even more connection attempts and retries” and “persistent congestion.”

Microsoft’s way out was to meter the recovery. Through Thursday night and into Friday, it walled off part of its infrastructure, restarted it, let a little traffic in, and watched whether it held before letting in more. It also added virtual machines, computers it can start up in software on its own hardware, to absorb the surge.

At 4:24 a.m. Eastern on Friday it extended its email timeout to 48 hours, “to help preserve delayed mail.” Mail servers that can't deliver a message keep retrying for a set period, then give up and bounce it back to the sender as undeliverable. Stretching that window to two days meant your Thursday afternoon email would wait in line instead of coming back to you with an error.

Recovery then went region by region: parts of Asia-Pacific first, then Europe, then North America. Kentik saw Exchange traffic start climbing at about 6:20 a.m. Eastern on Friday, and by 8:25 a.m. it was running about 19% above normal as queued mail and mailbox syncs caught up. That spike is your Thursday email landing, along with everyone else's. At 9:17 a.m. Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.”

At 1:05 p.m. on Friday, Microsoft explained the long tail in a statement that also apologized: “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.” The outage still wasn't over. By Friday evening The Register was counting past 27 hours.

That 1:05 p.m. statement also named a cause, briefly. Microsoft wrote that “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” that it had “addressed the underlying issue,” and that this “was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.” It promised “a full post-incident report once our review is complete.”

The statement doesn't say what went wrong in the upgrade, and it sits awkwardly beside Thursday's posts. At 3:19 p.m., Microsoft said it had “not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact.” About 80 minutes later it was assessing whether to revert “a small number of recent configuration updates.” By Friday, CIO reported it was reverting a network configuration change that “correlated with the start of the disruption.” The report will need to reconcile those three accounts.

Online, people had picked a cause well before Microsoft named one. The top comment on one large r/technology thread blamed AI-written code that nobody knew how to fix, which Microsoft’s statement now rules out. Others blamed layoffs, often with a figure of 60,000 jobs. The reporting I can find says Microsoft cut about 4,800 roles in July, about 2.1% of its workforce. It had also offered buyouts in April, to an undisclosed number of employees. Nothing I’ve found connects those cuts to this outage. Until the report is out, anyone telling you exactly why your email stopped on Thursday is guessing.

Michael Grothaus made the strongest objection to this account in Fast Company on Friday morning: “Such a long service interruption is rare for a platform as critical for communications and as large as Outlook,” especially one run by “a nearly $4 trillion company with nearly unlimited technical resources at its disposal.” Read that way, the thundering herd sounds like an alibi, since by Microsoft's own account what broke Exchange was an issue in its network upgrade.

The research backs him on the trigger. The OSDI study found that around 45% of the triggers in its sample were “engineer errors, such as buggy configuration or code deployments.” Microsoft has seen one of its own fixes make things worse before, too. In January, Microsoft 365 went down across North America for eight to ten hours, depending on whose count you use. TechRepublic reported that an early load-balancing adjustment “actually worsened the situation by creating additional traffic imbalances.”

After two outages at Azure Front Door, which routes traffic into much of its cloud, Microsoft published its lessons in December 2025. It said incompatible or erroneous configuration should “never propagate beyond canary environments.” A canary is the small slice of the system that gets every change first, so a bad change breaks something small. Microsoft added longer waits between rollout stages and a one-click revert to the last configuration known to work. It also admitted that during one of those October rollouts, the health-check validations “were all passed” while the problem spread. Those commitments covered Front Door, and nothing I’ve found shows Microsoft made the same ones for Exchange.

If retries did help keep Exchange down, part of that herd was Microsoft’s own software, because Outlook on phones and laptops is Microsoft’s code. Amazon's 2021 write-up admits the same thing about its own clients: they “have well tested request back-off behaviors,” it said, but “a latent issue prevented these clients from adequately backing off during this event.” Whether Microsoft’s clients backed off properly on Thursday night is a question its report can answer, because it wrote the clients.

Bronson and his co-authors wrote in 2021 that “It is common for an outage that involves a metastable failure to be initially blamed on the trigger, but the true root cause is the sustaining effect." The trigger is why Outlook went down on Thursday afternoon. If the pattern holds, the retries, the pulled servers and the herd are why it stayed down until Friday.

On the server side, the main defense is load shedding: a swamped server turns new work away quickly and politely, telling the client to come back later, instead of accepting everything and collapsing. The OSDI authors found load shedding was “the most popular mitigation effort used in over 50% of the incidents” they studied, and also that it's hard to get right, because without understanding the feedback loop, “it is hard to know just how much the load needs to be reduced.” Google's SRE book recommends the slow start Microsoft eventually used: “Gradually ramping up the load. This strategy allows caches to warm up, connections to be established.”

On the client side, the defense is backoff with jitter. Each failed attempt waits a little longer than the last, and the wait includes some randomness, so millions of devices don’t all try again in the same second. Brooker’s article walks through both the backoff and the randomness. Without the randomness, clients that failed together retry together.

Most of us don't run Exchange, and what we control is much smaller. Sanchit Vir Gogia, an analyst at Greyhound Research, told CIO that “Enterprises have priced Microsoft 365 as a licence and never as a single point of failure,” and that “The answer is not a second suite. It is a rehearsed fallback for the few things that cannot stop: an out-of-band channel for incident command, mail continuity for critical roles, and a written decision on whether each security control fails open or closed.”

I’ve said before that you don't own a business you can't switch back on yourself. Email is the exception nearly everyone accepts, since nobody is going to start running a mail server over one bad Thursday. What you can decide ahead of time is how the few things that can’t stop will keep going while email is down. Gogia’s three items make good questions for a team to answer in an afternoon, and the British police add a fourth:

On Thursday afternoon, Britain’s police already had theirs: call 101.

The video version of this story is on YouTube. If this was useful, there’s more, including my latest book, at davesaunders.net.

#9743. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9742. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9741. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

This entry was posted on Friday 9th of October 2026 08:17 PM

The irony here is hard to miss. The industry sells “communicating with a criminal isn’t the same as paying” as a clean distinction, but the line between negotiator and middleman gets blurry fast when the same people sit between victims and extortionists. Charges are only allegations at this point, but if the other firms Brian mentions get charged too, expect a lot more scrutiny of how ransomware negotiators operate and who they’re really accountable to.

It’s worse than ironic, it’s sadly common these days in most fields. Once the commercial motive is introduced, there’s a *huge* incentive for the people involved to perpetuate the problem rather than solve it. I think I first ran into it in the early days of the anti-spam efforts, where working solutions were sidelined in favor of poorly functioning technologies that mostly served to give monopoly players control of deliverability. The email phishing that leads to ransomware gangs like Shiny Hunters simply *would not happen* if people just wised up to the fact that these trillion dollar companies aren’t giving you technology advice that works in *your* best interest.

So the FBI got another low-level “dealer”. Great. Now let’s see how long it takes them to round up *anyone* from the Epstein-class “supplier” organizations.

The very least the FBI could do would be to post these filth hackass addresses, bank information, family records, social securities, phone numbers and what not, so they end up eaten alive by the same annoyance they created. Die by the sword bastards.

Somehow I doubt this government is providing any finders-fees for your work, keep up the good work Krebs.
